reasons: All five anchors read as quoted. They are all transmitted text: the claims file has no 'emended' marks (grep count 0). Arm. gorc = Gk ἔργον (*wérǵom) is a sound cognate, so the 'deed' member is cognate. The 'word' members are not cognate: Arm. ban (< *bʰeh₂-ni-) vs Gk λόγος. So the Armenian-Greek anchors share only one cognate element. The fully cognate inherited pair (Hom. ἔπος/ἔργον ~ Av. hūxta/huuaršta, both *wekʷ- + *werǵ-) is real; I opened the supporting loci and they check out: the Avestan triad at HN1.7a.6, Y35.2a and N66.4a, and the Homeric coordinations at Il. 1.504, Il. 15.234, Od. 2.272 and Hymn. Cer. 65 (ἔπει/ἔργῳ, ἔργον/ἔπος). On the Germanic side, Beo. 289 (worda/worca) also checks out. The Heliand coordination (uuordun/uuercun) is Christian Gospel-harmony diction and may follow Latin verbo/opere. But it is not shown by the Armenian anchors. Movsēs is a Hellenizing historian writing in the Greek λόγος/ἔργον topos; at p.1835 the phrase comes right after an explicit Platonic quotation. 'Word and deed' is also a constant Biblical/patristic pair (Luke 24:19, Col 3:17, 1 John 3:18; λόγῳ/ἔργῳ). The Armenian collocation is therefore best explained as a Greek-modelled cliché, not independent inheritance. The polar 'words and deeds' merism is itself highly generic. On their own, the Armenian anchors are derivative and would be a reject. The grade is weak only because the *werǵ- 'deed' member is independently attested in a congruent 'word and deed' pairing in Homeric Greek, Avestan and Old English (all checked), so the figure itself is real. The Armenian anchors add no independent evidence for it.

The etymologies hold: Arm. ayr (gen. aṙn) = Skt. nara- (*h₂nḗr), and Arm. ji = Skt. háya- (Martirosyan s.v. ji; vocalism problematic but the equation is standard). The collocation does not match. In Armenian, aṙn + jioy is a fixed collective idiom for 'troops, cavalry'. MBh 8.19.154 is not that idiom: it is one line of a battlefield catalogue (chariots and elephants in s153, horses and men in s154, the bloody earth in s155), a list of fallen army components, not a binomial merism. The Vedic support is misread: AVŚ 3.16.6 (= AVP 4.31.6) is a prayer for wealth (gobhir, aśvair, nṛbhir, nṛvantaḥ: increase in cows, horses and men), not an army. 'Men and horses' for an army is a universal pairing, also common in Biblical diction (horse and rider). Two cognate nouns that both mean basic military entities co-occur by chance in battle narrative. No 'emended' marks in the claims file (grep count 0).

The Armenian idiom is the very common jeṙn + arkanel 'set hand to, undertake; lay hands on'. In the corpus it occurs dozens of times, mostly without gorc: with i + object or with an infinitive (Koriwn, Ełišē, Pʻawstos, Agathangelos). It matches Greek ἐπιχειρεῖν / ἐπιβάλλειν + χεῖρας, the Biblical 'lay hands on' (e.g. Ełišē 991 quoting the Passion). The second Łazar anchor (p.2307), 'whatever work he set hand to, the Lord prospered in his hand', is a clear echo of Gen 39:3/23 (Joseph). Łazar repeats it at p.2370 (yaǰołēr with jeṙs). So it is Biblical, not inherited. The Euripides line (ἔργον, ἵεσαν, χέρας) is a generic image. Hand and work co-occur in any language. No 'emended' marks in the claims file (grep count 0).

reasons: Both anchors were read and are transmitted text. In the corpus, Arm. ołǰ + ler/lerukʻ occurs only as an epistolary salutation or closing inside quoted letters and edicts: Movsēs 1772, 1773, 1823, 1902, 2012 (twice), 2030, 2065, 2072, 2078, 2088, 2089 (twice), 2090; Agathangelos 1371, 1373, 1382, 1698. Movsēs 1903 (verb ołjam 'I wish' with infinitive linel) is a word-for-word rendering of the Greek letter formula 'I wish you to be well' (ἐρρῶσθαι + εὔχομαι). Ołǰ ler is therefore the Armenian rendering of the Greek epistolary ἔρρωσο / ἔρρωσθε (cf. Acts 15:29), with the native word 'whole' standing in for 'be strong'. That makes it derivative of a Greek model. Lat. salue in Plautus is a spoken meeting greeting, not an epistolary formula; the Latin letter equivalent is vale. Etymology: Lat. salvus < *solH-u-o- (de Vaan). For Arm. ołǰ, Martirosyan follows Meillet's *(s)ol-i̯o- and calls *solu̯-i̯o- unconvincing. So the root is cognate but the formations differ, and the claim's etymon *solh₂-u̯(i)o- is rejected by the dictionary cited, so the root is cognate but the stated formation is not. Wishing someone 'health/wholeness' as a greeting is cross-linguistically generic (OE hāl, Hebrew šalom).

known: The root equation Lat. salvus ~ Gk οὖλος/οὖλε ~ Skt. sárva- is standard (de Vaan s.v. salvus). The Od. 24.402 οὖλε greeting is a familiar comparandum. The Armenian letter formula is generally regarded as Greek epistolary convention.

reasons: All Armenian and Greek anchors were read and are transmitted text, but several do not fit the claimed formula. Łazar p.2211 w1/3 (anown with participle kočʻecʻeloy 'called') is a different construction (anown + 'called'). In Hdt. 2.181.2 the relative τῇ refers to the daughter Ladike, not to ἀνδρός. Hdt. 3.120.2 has no ἀνήρ ('another Persian') and uses the infinitive εἶναι in reported speech. Only Łazar w2/3 ('son of a man to whom the name was Vardan') and Hdt. 4.161.2 / 1.96.1 fit. The Armenian type (orowm + anown + ēr + name) is very frequent in Koriwn, Pʻawstos and others; it is the Armenian Bible's standard rendering of LXX/NT ᾧ/ᾗ + ὄνομα (e.g. Luke 1:26-27, 'to a man whose name was Joseph'). The Armenian historians therefore carry a Biblical-Greek calque. In addition, a naming clause with a dative possessor ('to whom the name was', Lat. cui + nomen) is a generic Indo-European and non-IE device. The individual cognates are right: ayr = ἀνήρ, anown = ὄνομα, ēr from *h₁es-. But the collocation is derivative and generic. No 'emended' marks in the claims file (grep count 0).
